# Audio-master timing — why the audio clock drives the game

Most browser games use `requestAnimationFrame` as their master
clock. Phosphor 78 doesn't. Our master clock is the AudioContext;
the rendering loop is its slave. Here's why.

## The two clocks

A modern browser has two relevant clocks:

```svg
<svg viewBox="0 0 600 220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="diagram">
  <defs>
    <marker id="arrow3" viewBox="0 0 8 8" refX="6" refY="4" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0,0 L8,4 L0,8 z" fill="#00ff66" />
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <g font-family="monospace" font-size="11" fill="#ddd" text-anchor="middle">
    <rect x="20" y="20" width="200" height="60" fill="#220" stroke="#ffaa00" rx="4" />
    <text x="120" y="42">requestAnimationFrame</text>
    <text x="120" y="58">~16.6 ms</text>
    <text x="120" y="72" fill="#ffaa00" font-size="10">±1-3 ms jitter</text>
    <rect x="380" y="20" width="200" height="60" fill="#143" stroke="#00ff66" rx="4" />
    <text x="480" y="42">AudioContext.currentTime</text>
    <text x="480" y="58">~22 µs precision</text>
    <text x="480" y="72" fill="#00ff66" font-size="10">sample-accurate</text>
    <line x1="220" y1="50" x2="375" y2="50" stroke="#888" stroke-dasharray="3 3" />
    <text x="300" y="42" fill="#888" font-size="10">two parallel clocks</text>
    <text x="300" y="62" fill="#888" font-size="10">on different threads</text>
    <rect x="190" y="130" width="220" height="60" fill="#143" stroke="#00ff66" rx="4" />
    <text x="300" y="160">audio is master, rAF is slave</text>
    <line x1="480" y1="80" x2="380" y2="130" stroke="#00ff66" marker-end="url(#arrow3)" />
    <line x1="120" y1="80" x2="220" y2="130" stroke="#888" stroke-dasharray="3 3" marker-end="url(#arrow3)" />
    <text x="300" y="210" fill="#888">The frame loop reads the audio clock; never the other way around.</text>
  </g>
</svg>
```

`requestAnimationFrame` runs at the display refresh rate — usually
60 Hz, sometimes 120 Hz, occasionally 1 Hz when the tab is hidden. Its
callbacks are best-effort: the browser tries to call them at
vsync, but a busy main thread can push them by milliseconds and
the tab being deprioritized can stall them indefinitely.

`AudioContext.currentTime` is sample-accurate. It advances at the
audio sample rate (typically 48 kHz) and is generated by the audio
thread, which the OS prioritizes higher than the JS main thread.
No matter what the main thread is doing, the audio clock keeps
ticking precisely.

## Why audio-master matters for Space Invaders

Space Invaders' march tempo is more than a sound effect — it's a
game mechanic. The 4-step descending pitch loop accelerates as
aliens die, communicating game state through the listener's sense
of rhythm. If the march tempo wobbled by even 50 ms per note,
veterans of the original would notice immediately.

Driving the march from `requestAnimationFrame` would mean each
note's trigger time inherits the rAF jitter — easily +/- 16 ms
under main-thread load. Driving it from the audio clock means each
note's trigger time is sample-accurate regardless of what the
renderer is doing.

## The lookahead scheduler

There's a classic Web Audio pattern (Chris Wilson, _A Tale of
Two Clocks_) for sample-accurate event scheduling: rather than
triggering each event when the moment arrives, schedule events
into AudioContext's near-future every few milliseconds.

```svg
<svg viewBox="0 0 600 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="diagram">
  <g font-family="monospace" font-size="11">
    <text x="20" y="20" fill="#888">Audio clock timeline (right = future)</text>
    <line x1="20" y1="80" x2="580" y2="80" stroke="#888" />
    <!-- Tick marks every 100ms -->
    <g stroke="#444" stroke-width="1">
      <line x1="80"  y1="76" x2="80"  y2="84" />
      <line x1="160" y1="76" x2="160" y2="84" />
      <line x1="240" y1="76" x2="240" y2="84" />
      <line x1="320" y1="76" x2="320" y2="84" />
      <line x1="400" y1="76" x2="400" y2="84" />
      <line x1="480" y1="76" x2="480" y2="84" />
    </g>
    <!-- "Now" marker -->
    <line x1="80" y1="50" x2="80" y2="110" stroke="#00ff66" stroke-width="2" />
    <text x="80" y="44" fill="#00ff66" text-anchor="middle">now</text>
    <!-- Lookahead window -->
    <rect x="80" y="60" width="100" height="40" fill="#143" opacity="0.5" />
    <text x="130" y="55" fill="#00ff66" text-anchor="middle">lookahead 100ms</text>
    <!-- Future scheduled events -->
    <g fill="#ffaa00">
      <circle cx="100" cy="80" r="4" />
      <circle cx="135" cy="80" r="4" />
      <circle cx="165" cy="80" r="4" />
    </g>
    <text x="130" y="125" fill="#ffaa00" text-anchor="middle">events queued ahead</text>
    <text x="130" y="138" fill="#ffaa00" text-anchor="middle">via setValueAtTime</text>
    <text x="20" y="170" fill="#888">Every 25ms a poll runs and schedules anything that should fire in the next 100ms.</text>
  </g>
</svg>
```

Phosphor 78's `audio/clock.ts` exposes:

- `currentTime` — pass-through to `audioContext.currentTime`.
- `currentStep(N)` — given N alive aliens, returns the
  current march-step index. Pure function of `currentTime`.
- `lookaheadUntil()` — returns `currentTime + 100ms`.
- `scheduleAhead(fn)` — calls `fn(until)` so callers can enqueue
  events whose trigger time is `<= until`.

The polling cadence is 25 ms (small enough to keep the lookahead
window full), the lookahead window is 100 ms (small enough that
pause-resume responds within ~2 frames, large enough to absorb
typical setTimeout jitter).

## Reading the audio clock from the frame loop

The renderer doesn't know or care how the audio clock works. Each
frame the game loop reads `audioClock.currentTime` once, passes
it into the reducer, and the reducer uses it to decide what step
the march is on:

```javascript
const { next, events } = tick(state, input, audioClock);
state = next;
events.forEach((e) => audioEngine.handle(e));
```

`tick` is a pure function of `(state, input, clock)`. Same inputs
always produce the same outputs. The `clock` argument is the only
non-deterministic source — and it's deterministic given a real
audio clock; only the _display_ refresh rate is jittery.

## The disassembly's tempo table — and a famous bug

The original 1978 ROM has a table at addresses `$1A11` and `$1A21`
that maps remaining alien count to an inter-note interval, in
60 Hz interrupt ticks:

| Alive aliens (>=) | Interval (interrupts) | Interval (ms) |
| ----------------: | --------------------: | ------------: |
|                50 |                    52 |           867 |
|                43 |                    46 |           767 |
|                36 |                    39 |           650 |
|                28 |                    34 |           567 |
|                22 |                    28 |           467 |
|                17 |                    24 |           400 |
|                13 |                    21 |           350 |
|                10 |                    19 |           317 |
|                 8 |                    16 |           267 |
|                 7 |                    14 |           233 |
|                 6 |                    13 |           217 |
|                 5 |                    12 |           200 |
|                 4 |                    11 |           183 |
|                 3 |                     9 |           150 |
|                 2 |                     7 |           117 |
|                 1 |                     5 |            83 |

That table is encoded bit-for-bit into
`src/constants/computer-archeology.ts` as `MARCH_TEMPO_TABLE`. The
audio clock's `currentStep()` uses it.

There's a separate, more famous bug in the saucer-scoring table
at ROM `$1D54`: the wrap-check uses `< $63` instead of `< $64`,
so the 16th byte of a 16-byte score-cycle table is never read.
The cycle is effectively 15 long, and entry 8 (the 9th hit) gives
300 points. That's where the famous "every 15 saucer hits = 300"
pattern comes from. Phosphor 78 reproduces that bug exactly,
because it's a load-bearing feature of the original.

## The acceleration curve

The mapping from alive aliens to inter-note interval looks like
this:

```svg
<svg viewBox="0 0 600 220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="diagram">
  <g font-family="monospace" font-size="11">
    <line x1="40" y1="190" x2="580" y2="190" stroke="#888" />
    <line x1="40" y1="20"  x2="40"  y2="190" stroke="#888" />
    <text x="20" y="22"  fill="#888" text-anchor="middle">900</text>
    <text x="20" y="190" fill="#888" text-anchor="middle">0</text>
    <text x="40" y="210" fill="#888" text-anchor="middle">55</text>
    <text x="580" y="210" fill="#888" text-anchor="middle">1</text>
    <text x="310" y="210" fill="#888" text-anchor="middle">aliens alive</text>
    <text x="20" y="100" fill="#888" text-anchor="middle" transform="rotate(-90, 20, 100)">interval (ms)</text>
    <!-- Step plot of the table values. We map alien count [55,1] to x=[40,580]
         and interval [0,900] to y=[190,20]. -->
    <polyline fill="none" stroke="#00ff66" stroke-width="2"
      points="40,30
              90,30 90,49
              160,49 160,69
              230,69 230,90
              290,90 290,114
              350,114 350,131
              400,131 400,148
              450,148 450,160
              490,160 490,174
              510,174 510,176
              530,176 530,178
              540,178 540,180
              550,180 550,182
              560,182 560,184
              570,184 570,186
              580,186" />
    <text x="490" y="20" fill="#00ff66">geometric, not linear</text>
  </g>
</svg>
```

The slope is steep at the start (each alien killed shaves a lot
of time off the next note), then flattens (later kills shave
proportionally less). Combined with the 4-note loop you cycle
through, this is what gives the late game its frantic, almost
panicked feel — the kind of feel that's hard to describe in
words but instantly recognizable when you hear it.

## Try the visualizer above

The N slider above lets you scrub through the alien-count range
and watch the inter-note interval drop from 867 ms down to 83 ms. At
the start of a wave a note plays roughly once a second; by the
end you're hearing them four times a second. The acceleration is
geometric, not linear — that's why it feels frantic.
